analysis.one_liner: Phases out federal sugar price supports and crop quotas that keep U.S. sugar prices above world levels.
analysis.headline: Introduced by Senator Schumer with six Republican and two Democratic cosponsors, the bill never left the Senate Agriculture Committee and died without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law guarantees sugar growers and processors loans at fixed prices and controls who can plant sugar through marketing quotas. This bill would have lowered those guaranteed loan rates year by year, converted them to loans processors must repay, ended all sugar price support after the 2002 crop, and repealed the planting quotas. It would also have directed the President to keep U.S. sugar prices no higher than the world price or the federal loan rate.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers, who pay above-world prices for sugar and sugar-containing foods under the current program, and food manufacturers — candy makers, bakers, cereal makers — that buy sugar as a main ingredient.

how_it_helps.text: Lowers the guaranteed raw cane sugar loan rate step by step, from 18 cents per pound to 14 cents by the 2002 crop.
Converts the loans to recourse loans, meaning sugar processors must repay them rather than the government keeping their sugar when prices fall.
Ends all federal price support for the 2003 and later crops of sugarcane and sugar beets, ending subsidies and government market operations for sugar entirely.
Repeals the sugar and crystalline fructose marketing quotas and acreage allotments that restrict who can grow sugar.
Directs the President to ensure raw sugar is available to the U.S. market at no more than the higher of the world price or the federal loan rate, keeping a ceiling on consumer prices.

analysis.who_pays: Sugarcane and sugar beet growers and processors, who would lose guaranteed prices well above the world market level, quota-protected market shares, and then all support after 2002. The bill contains no transition assistance for them.

drawbacks.text: Growers would see their guaranteed price fall from 18 cents to 14 cents per pound over four crops and disappear entirely after 2002, exposing them to volatile world prices.
Repealing the marketing quotas removes the supply-control system sugar growers have operated under for decades, a major change to their business model.
The bill provides no transition payments or adjustment aid for growers and rural communities dependent on sugar production during the phase-out.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill spreads the cost of ending the sugar program gradually over four crop years, which softens the blow to growers. The main weakness is that it offers nothing to help growers adjust during the phase-out — the benefit to consumers is real but the burden lands on a specific farming sector with no cushion. A well-designed version might have paired the phase-out with temporary adjustment support.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee in May 1999, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Senator Schumer introduced the bill on May 25, 1999 with five original cosponsors from both parties, including Democrats Feinstein and Moynihan and Republicans Chafee, Gregg, and Santorum.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry on the day it was introduced.
The committee took no further action on the bill; no markup, no committee report, and no Senate vote appear in its action history for the rest of the Congress.
The bill received eight cosponsors in total, six Republicans and two Democrats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sugar growers and processors kept the price support program and marketing quotas that hold U.S. sugar prices above world levels; consumers kept paying the difference.

sides.party_line_note: Support crossed party lines — of the bill's eight cosponsors, six were Republicans and two were Democrats — but the bill died in committee with no roll-call vote on either side.

industries.industry: Sugarcane and sugar beet growers and processors
industries.note: The program guarantees them loan rates well above the world sugar price and restricts planting through quotas; when processors default, the government keeps their sugar, propping up prices. The bill would have cut those rates by 2002 and ended all support and quotas after that, shifting the cost of above-market sugar from consumers back to the industry.

Sugar is a major input cost for these industries, and U.S. prices run above world levels under the support program. The bill's requirement that sugar be available at no more than the world price or the loan rate would have lowered their input costs and, eventually, food prices.
